Pañcatantra
C. 100-500 A. D. collection of popular fables, stories etc. interspersed with moral an. educative verses; in 5 sections; original text not avaliable; earliest available text ascribed to Viṣṇuśarman or Somaśarman, patronised by king Amaraśakti of Mahilāropya; first rendered into Pahlavi (not extant); then into Persian an. Arabic under the name Kalileh vah Damne; translated into Greek by Symeon (end of 11th Cent.); into Turkish in 16th Cent. by Ali-binSāliḥ; abridged versions are found in Bṛhatkathāmañjarī an. Kathāsaritsāgara.
The well known recensions an. versions of Pañcatantra are: [Page014-b]
(1) Pañcākhyāna of Pūrṇabhadra.
(2) Pañcākhyānoddhāra.
(3) Hitopadeśa (recast) of Nārāyaṇa.
(4) Tantrākhyāyikā (Kashmirian).
(5) Tantropākhyāna of Vasubhāga. For this see IHQ. X. p.. 104-11.
Many versions in South Indian languages are also available.
See G. T. Artola, Pañcatantra Mss. from S. I., Adyar Libr. Bulletin XXXI. p.. 185-262; also L. Alsdorf, Pantschatantra, Bergen, 1952; R. Gelb, Zur Frage nach der Urfassung des Pañcatantra, Wiesbaden, 1968.
Translated into most of the languages of the world. See Wint. HIL. III. i. p.. 329-46. For details see Intro. to Hertel's edn. of Pañcatantra, HOS. 11. 12 an. 14. For a table on transl.. into diff. languages see Tawney & Penzer, Ocean of Stories X. p.. 232-42.
For a list of mss. of the following versions see also Intro. to Hertel's edn. HOS. 12.
1. Tantropākhyāna of Vasubhāga p.. 36-41.
2. Pañcatantra of Viṣṇuśarman p.. 8-30.
3. Hitopaḍeśa of Nārāyaṇa p.. 30-35.
-- identity of version not known.
